title: Do Disguised-as-Deployment Prompts Lower Measured Safety vs Honeypot Prompts?

original_idea.body:
# Do Disguised-as-Deployment Prompts Lower Measured Safety vs Honeypot Prompts?

**Problem:** Apollo's anti-scheming work and probing studies both suggest obvious test framing inflates apparent safety. A clean follow-up: directly measure, on open models, how much misaligned-behavior rates rise when the SAME scenario is rewritten to look like realistic deployment rather than an obvious eval.

**Direction:** Author matched scenario pairs differing only in 'eval-ness' (one explicitly framed as a safety test/honeypot, one rewritten as a mundane realistic task with identical incentives). Run small open models and measure the gap in covert-action / harmful-compliance rates between the two framings. Success = a quantified 'realism penalty' showing how much safety evals overstate alignment when they look like tests.

**Why it matters:** Provides a concrete estimate of how much current evals over-report safety due to eval-recognition — a methodology correction the field urgently needs and that requires only prompt engineering plus open models.

**Relevant context:** arXiv:2509.15541 notes results complicated by eval-recognition; arXiv:2507.01786 found safety evals look artificial; Apollo eval-awareness work documents honeypot detection.
